title: Defence Medical Services: capacity, risks and the gaps to NATO standards
label: 27 October 2026 · One-off session on Defence Medical Services
summary: Former Surgeon-Generals Martin Bricknell and Timothy Hodgetts told the Defence Committee that the UK's Defence Medical Services (DMS) have been hollowed out: clinical quality and doctrine are good, but capacity across evacuation, hospitals, logistics and workforce is inadequate for high-intensity war. They set out five main risks, welcomed some investment and reforms but warned current funding and plans fall far short of allied examples. They urged national-level planning, exercises with the NHS, better data and multinational cooperation.

speakers.label: Maj Gen Hodgetts
speakers.name: Timothy Hodgetts
speakers.role: Former Surgeon General and ex-Chair, NATO Committee of Chiefs of Military Medical Services

glossary.definition: The UK's military medical organisation that provides healthcare to service personnel and supports operations.
The Strategic Defence Review chapter that covered medical services and recommended changes; witnesses refer to it as 'SDR'.
NATO's plan, agreed by members, identifying weaknesses and actions to prepare military medical services for high-intensity conflict.
Medical evacuation with ongoing care en route, usually in protected ambulances or aircraft.
Casualty evacuation without ongoing medical treatment – moving patients from point of wounding.
Defence Primary Healthcare, the military's primary care system that keeps personnel fit and returns them to duty.
Reception arrangements for military patients arriving into the civilian hospital system in the UK.
NATO Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, the body that set the medical manifesto and action plan.
MOD spending plan; witnesses noted a £50m DMS allocation over four years.
The UK commitment to support service personnel; witnesses discussed its relevance to healthcare provision.

chapters.title: State of the Service
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses say the DMS has been 'hollowed out'—clinical expertise and doctrine are strong, but capacity and infrastructure are too small for high‑intensity war.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Jopp
turns.text: Gen. Barrons called DMS 'the most hollowed-out bit of defence'—do you agree?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: Yes. When we reviewed DMS for the SDR, we found sustained pressures over 15 years. Clinically the UK is good, but baseline capacity to scale up in war is at risk.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: I’d frame it as five main risks for casualties at scale: medical evacuation, mass casualty planning, medical logistics, regulatory/legal freedoms, and workforce shortages.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Jopp
turns.text: Has the SDR taken these problems on board?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: The SDR included our key recommendations on paper, but delivery and funding are different matters.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Jopp
turns.text: Where does the DMS sit in the Defence structure now?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: It’s now called Defence Medical Command under CSOC—there's some centralisation, but other NATO countries have gone further.

chapters.title: The five operational risks
chapters.takeaway: Medevacs, mass-casualty plans, supply chains, legal/regulatory readiness, and workforce shortfalls are the critical failure points in high-intensity conflict.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: First: medevac—protected vehicles to move wounded to timely surgery. If that fails, avoidable deaths rise because most preventable deaths happen before hospital.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Second: mass casualty planning—military theatre plans must prioritise returning people to duty; civilian major-incident plans are different and can’t just be copied.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Third: medical logistics. Covid showed just-in-time supplies fail in crises; we must hold more stock and decide what to onshore.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Fourth: legal and regulatory freedoms—pre-authorise cross‑national credentialing, blood and drug use between allies, and faster approvals for innovation in conflict.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Fifth: workforce—we lack enough military medical personnel to run training, readiness and a large casualty load at the same time.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which of these is the largest gap for the UK?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: Overall: capacity across the whole enterprise—from frontline evacuation platforms to hospital beds and trained staff.

chapters.title: Workforce, training and surge capacity
chapters.takeaway: Surge capacity is the main constraint: training a surgeon takes 15 years, reserves and 'sponsored' arrangements can help but need a national workforce plan.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: Where are the pinch points in staffing?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: DMS should use a whole-force model—regulars, reserves and civilian partners—but money, post-attribution and recruitment remain problems.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Most of our capability is people. Clinical posts have been civilianised or cut; surgical capacity is a critical pinch point.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: How long to train an orthopaedic surgeon?

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: About 15 years from medical school to consultant; GP about 10 years. You can't rapidly create specialists from scratch.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: Can sponsored reserves or commercial teams plug gaps?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: We recommended a DMS workforce plan in the SDR to examine sponsored reserves and civilian partnerships; we haven't seen the published plan yet.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Sponsored reserves and multinational medical teams are valuable. For example, contracts with private providers or ISOS could supply formed clinical teams.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Also note positive organisational moves: the Royal Army Medical Service merged three corps to increase flexibility, and skills training for medics has expanded.

chapters.title: Civilian–military integration: NHS, data and research
chapters.takeaway: Clinical guidelines and research partnerships exist, but the NHS needs exercises, shared data systems, and more primary-care investment to handle mass casualties.

turns.speaker: Michelle Scrogham
turns.text: What planning will stop the NHS collapsing if reservists are called?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: The NHS is huge, so overall demand may be manageable, but there will be pinch points—burns, plastics, and specialist surgery. We need joint planning and exercises like allies have done.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: On treatment guidance: military operational guidelines were adapted in 2017 into NHS mass-casualty guidance and distributed to trusts; those guidelines were shared with NATO in 2023.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Problem: many civilian clinicians haven't seen or exercised those guidelines. We need more joint exercises so people know how to treat blast and ballistic injuries.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Data is crucial—from point of injury through NHS care to rehab. Good data drove the huge outcome improvements in Iraq and Afghanistan and would help in future.

turns.speaker: Michelle Scrogham
turns.text: Is primary-care infrastructure being upgraded?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: The Care Quality Commission has noted organisational improvements but flagged infrastructure weaknesses across defence primary healthcare. SDR didn’t fund that explicitly.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Research links—blood research with the MRC, blast brain-injury work with Birmingham—are important to improving outcomes and must be sustained.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: On operational effect: Defence Primary Healthcare has cut some waiting times—ENT from ~17 to 12 weeks, trauma and orthopaedics from ~14 to 10 weeks—showing targeted changes can help return people to duty.

chapters.title: Scale, NATO comparisons and what must change
chapters.takeaway: The UK can deploy effective clinical teams now but lacks the scale for mass casualties; allied investments show how much more is needed in protected infrastructure, platforms and stockpiles.

turns.speaker: Jesse Norman
turns.text: Afghanistan and Iraq caseloads were relatively small. If we faced hundreds of casualties a day, are we overwhelmed?

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Yes. Typical large bursts then were about 10 casualties; modern scenarios could be orders of magnitude larger. Germany is planning for about 1,000 troop casualties per day.

turns.speaker: Jesse Norman
turns.text: Has the MOD planned for that scale?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: We urged planning in the SDR. Some work is underway, but there is little visible public evidence of a complete plan to close the gaps.

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: If we lose air superiority and cannot use helicopters, how will evacuation work across Europe?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: You need a theatre-level plan: how a casualty moves from point of wounding to a strategic hub and then to the UK—ambulance trains, ferries, protected vehicles and multinational support will all be needed.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Regulation matters—movement of blood and drugs often uses EU derogations; we must ensure UK rules align with NATO and EU partners to accept allied supplies and clinicians treating each other's patients.

turns.speaker: Ian Roome
turns.text: Is current investment enough for the SDSR objectives?

turns.speaker: Lt Gen Bricknell
turns.text: The public Defence Investment Plan allocation was £50m over four years: a start but small compared with other allies. No clear funding for primary healthcare upgrades was visible.

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Allies are investing more: Germany ~€570m for protected forward medical infrastructure, Australia ~$420m for a medical services refresh, Estonia ~€150m for modular systems. Our current unit of deployable hospital is now a 48-bed field hospital vs Cold War 400–800.

turns.speaker: Mike Martin
turns.text: Can NATO share casualties between member hospitals?

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Yes—multinational medical facilities and reciprocal treatment are proven and should be used to buy out capability gaps, but interoperability and mutual legal arrangements must be in place.

turns.speaker: Derek Twigg
turns.text: What about mental health demand—PTSD and breakdown?

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: Mental health often represents 20–30% of non-battle injuries; it must be treated as far forward as possible. We need to plan for this volume in any surge.

turns.speaker: Emma Lewell
turns.text: Are we ready to deter or respond to a possible 2030 attack?

turns.speaker: Maj Gen Hodgetts
turns.text: We can deploy effective teams now, but our capacity to sustain large numbers of casualties is limited; that is the key vulnerability to fix.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If there’s anything you want to add, please send written evidence. Thank you both very much for your time.
